title: NorthC Almere Data Center Fire: A Compartment Blaze That Took Out the Facility Power Plant and Rippled Across Dutch Public Services

severity.usersAffected: Undisclosed headcount; multi-sector impact documented by named victims (Utrecht University, Statistics Netherlands/CBS, Transdev bus & tram, water board De Stichtse Rijnlanden, Surf, IBM Cloud AMS03, and GP/healthcare practices)
severity.impactUsd: Not published; facility owner Keppel DC REIT stated the incident was not expected to have a material impact on FY2026 distribution per unit; no damages, insurance, or customer-loss figure disclosed
servicesDown: Utrecht University network/applications/websites and access passes
Water board Hoogheemraadschap De Stichtse Rijnlanden network
GP practices' patient-record, scheduling and contact systems

brief: On 7 May 2026 (around 08:45 local time) a fire broke out in a rear technical compartment of NorthC's Almere data center (Rondebeltweg) that houses power infrastructure. No servers or data carriers caught fire, but the blaze burned part of the facility's power supply and the site lost power entirely — the compute survived, yet everything went dark, and NorthC ultimately had to rebuild the power plant with new transformers and UPS. (Published reporting says only that 'part of the power supply burnt down'; that BOTH the normal and standby feeds were lost is an engineering inference from the total, multi-day power loss and the full rebuild, not an official finding.) Because multiple Dutch organizations host critical systems there, the outage cascaded outward: Utrecht University, Statistics Netherlands (CBS), public-transport operator Transdev, a regional water board, research-ICT provider Surf, IBM Cloud's Amsterdam 03, and numerous GP practices all lost service. The fire was scaled down to GRIP 1 at 20:50 that evening and to GRIP 0 with the building partially released to NorthC teams at 00:35 on 8 May, kicking off a phased restoration estimated at up to 72 hours. Temporary redundant power and cooling were activated on 13 May, roughly a week after the fire. Grid power came back building-by-building over the following weeks, with Building 1's full utility-plus-standby topology targeted for 17 July 2026. The root cause remains officially undetermined; a draft cause report was only expected at end-September 2026 because the fire-damaged structure had to be secured first.

magnitude.note: Blast radius is high because the failure reached across sectors of Dutch public life (higher education, national statistics, public transport, water management, healthcare, cloud) from a single site. Users and duration are high (multi-day facility power loss, weeks to full grid). Financial score is a mid-band estimate held down by the absence of any published damages figure and the owner's 'no material FY2026 DPU impact' statement; the true operational and tenant cost is undisclosed.

sequenceOfEvents.event: A fire starts around 08:45 in a rear technical compartment of the Almere facility (Rondebeltweg) that houses power infrastructure. No IT/server hall is reported to have burned.
On-site personnel are evacuated in time; contemporaneous reporting notes it was not yet clear how many companies were experiencing technical issues.

The fire burns part of the facility's power supply in the rear technical compartment, causing a total loss of power at the site; no servers or data carriers caught fire. The site remained without power until temporary supply was stood up, and NorthC later rebuilt with new transformers and UPS — indicating both the normal and standby feeds were knocked out. (Press reported only that 'part of the power supply burnt down'; the both-feeds/redundancy-defeat reading is an engineering inference from the recovery record.)

sequenceOfEvents.event: Because power is cut, tenant organizations lose their systems: Utrecht University (closed Friday, digital systems and access passes down), Statistics Netherlands (CBS), Transdev bus and tram services, water board De Stichtse Rijnlanden, Surf members, IBM Cloud AMS03, and GP practices lose access to patient records, appointments and contact numbers.
The Veiligheidsregio (safety region) issues an all-clear, telling residents who could no longer smell smoke they could reopen their windows, standing down the earlier shelter warning.
The fire is scaled down to GRIP 1, indicating the incident is being brought under control.

The situation is further scaled down to GRIP 0 and the building is partially released, allowing NorthC teams to begin restoration work. In the following daytime update, phased power/cooling restoration is estimated to take up to 72 hours.
Temporary, redundant power and cooling are successfully activated, roughly a week after the fire (a ~six-day facility outage window).
Building 2 is reconnected to grid power (its technical room was not damaged).
The first portion of Building 1 is projected for grid reconnection.

Scheduled full reconnection of Building 1 to the regular grid with emergency generators as backup, restoring intended utility-plus-standby topology after new transformers and UPS installation. Execution on this date was not independently confirmed.
Independent-expert investigation and demolition of the fire-damaged structure scheduled, with possible follow-up in early September; a draft cause report is expected by end-September 2026.

rootCause: Officially undetermined. As of the late-July 2026 update, NorthC had not established the cause of the fire. The on-site technical investigation could not safely begin until the fire-damaged structure was secured and water-supply work completed, so independent-expert investigation and demolition were scheduled for 27 July to 7 August 2026 and a draft cause report was pushed to end-September 2026. What is established is the failure's effect rather than its origin: a fire in a rear technical compartment burned part of the facility's power supply and produced a total facility power loss even though no servers caught fire. Published reporting states only that 'part of the power supply burnt down'; that the fire knocked out both the normal and standby feeds is inferred from the total, multi-day loss of power and the subsequent rebuild with new transformers and UPS, not from an official finding.
contributingFactors: The fire originated in a rear technical compartment housing power infrastructure, placing the ignition source directly among the assets whose loss would take the whole site down.

The site suffered a total, multi-day power loss and had to be rebuilt with new transformers and UPS, which indicates the normal and standby power paths were both knocked out by the one event — an inference from the recovery record, since published press reported only that 'part of the power supply burnt down.'
Multiple tenants relied on facility power without independent local generation or geographic failover, so a site-level power loss translated directly into their service outages.
The fire caused structural damage severe enough that the building had to be secured and water-supply work completed before investigators could safely enter, delaying root-cause analysis by months.

Critical public-sector workloads (national statistics, healthcare records, public transport, water management) were concentrated at a single facility, amplifying the societal blast radius of one site's outage.

lessonsLearnt: A single compartment fire produced a total, multi-day facility power loss requiring a full power-plant rebuild — apparent evidence that co-locating primary and backup power lets one event defeat the redundancy, though the both-feeds reading is inferred from the recovery record rather than an official finding.
A facility-level power loss cascades immediately to any tenant that lacks independent local generation or an alternate site; the fire never touched the servers, yet the servers still went dark.

Concentrating critical public services — national statistics, healthcare records, public transport, water management, higher education — in one data center turns a single-site incident into a nationwide disruption.

When a fire causes structural damage, root-cause analysis can be delayed by months because investigators cannot safely enter until the building is secured, so incident communications must manage a long 'cause unknown' period.
Transparency gaps compound impact: the absence of a published affected-customer count or per-organization outage figures leaves affected users and the public without a clear picture of scope.
improvements: Physically separate and fire-compartmentalize the primary and backup power paths so no single fire zone can destroy both, and review detection/suppression coverage in technical/power compartments.
Encourage or require geographic redundancy and disaster-recovery failover for tenants running critical public-sector workloads, rather than single-site dependency.
Establish clearer, faster public impact reporting (tenant/customer scope, outage windows) during and after major incidents.

Harden and stage the power-restoration sequence (temporary power/cooling first, then per-building grid, then full utility-plus-standby topology) with pre-provisioned transformers and UPS to shorten recovery.
Conduct a post-incident structural/safety review so that future fire-damaged sites can be entered and investigated sooner, shortening the time to root cause.

comprehensiveAnalysis.heading: Failure mechanism: a power-plant fire, not a server fire
comprehensiveAnalysis.body: The defining feature of this incident is that the IT load never burned — the fire was in a rear technical compartment that housed power infrastructure, and it burned part of the facility's power supply, producing a total loss of power. The servers were physically intact but electrically dead. This inverts the usual mental model of a data center fire (racks ablaze) and points instead to the power plant as the single most concentrated point of failure: lose it, and a fully healthy compute estate becomes worthless. Published reporting confirms only that 'part of the power supply burnt down'; that both the normal and standby feeds were lost is inferred from the total, multi-day outage and the need to rebuild with new transformers and UPS. Because the root cause is officially undetermined, the mechanism of ignition remains unknown pending the end-September 2026 draft report.

comprehensiveAnalysis.heading: Why it cascaded across Dutch public life
comprehensiveAnalysis.body: The outage propagated because of dependency concentration, not because the fire spread. Numerous organizations run production systems at the Almere site with no evident local generation or cross-site failover, so a facility power loss became their outage instantly. The victim list is unusually broad for a single building — Utrecht University (down to access passes), Statistics Netherlands, Transdev's buses and trams, a regional water board, Surf's research-ICT members, IBM Cloud's Amsterdam 03, and GP practices locked out of patient records and appointment data. The societal reach came from who was hosted there, turning an infrastructure event into a public-services event.

comprehensiveAnalysis.heading: Recovery: staged over days to weeks
comprehensiveAnalysis.body: Recovery followed a deliberate ladder. The emergency was controlled the same evening — safety-region all-clear at 20:13 and GRIP 1 at 20:50 on 7 May — and the building was scaled to GRIP 0 and partially released to NorthC teams at 00:35 on 8 May with a phased restoration estimated at up to 72 hours. Temporary redundant power and cooling were activated on 13 May, roughly a week later, in what reporting framed as a six-day facility outage. Durable grid power then came back building-by-building: Building 2 in the week of 25 May, Building 1 partially by end June, with full utility-plus-standby topology (new transformers and UPS, generators as backup) targeted for 17 July 2026 — a date announced in the operator log but not independently confirmed as executed.

comprehensiveAnalysis.heading: Organizational and systemic factors
comprehensiveAnalysis.body: Two systemic issues stand out. First, redundancy appears to have been defeated by proximity: the total, multi-day power loss and full rebuild imply the primary and backup power were vulnerable to the same event, so the architecture that should have survived a single failure did not (an inference, since press reported only that 'part of the power supply burnt down'). Second, critical national functions were concentrated at one facility with insufficient tenant-side resilience, so the blast radius was national. The record also shows a transparency and investigation lag — no affected-customer count, per-organization outage duration, or damages figure was ever published, and the cause report was delayed to end-September 2026 because the damaged structure had to be secured before investigators could safely enter.

comprehensiveAnalysis.heading: Cross-incident pattern: the concentrated-power single point of failure
comprehensiveAnalysis.body: This event rhymes with a recurring class of data center outages in which the compute is fine but a shared upstream utility — power distribution, cooling, or a single electrical room — fails and takes everything with it. The lesson repeats across the industry: redundancy only counts if the redundant paths are independent in space and failure mode, and tenant resilience cannot be outsourced entirely to a single facility. The Almere fire is a particularly clean example because the servers demonstrably survived, isolating the failure to the power plant and the dependency graph hanging off it.

technicalDeepDive: The Almere event is best understood as a power-domain failure with an intact IT domain. A fire in a rear technical compartment — the space carrying the facility's power infrastructure — burned part of the power supply and collapsed the site's usable power to zero available feeds, keeping the site dark until a temporary redundant supply was stood up on 13 May. Published reporting states only that 'part of the power supply burnt down' and that no servers or data carriers caught fire; that the event removed both the normal (utility-fed) path and the standby (generator/UPS) path is an engineering inference from the total, multi-day loss of power and the subsequent rebuild — had a standby source survived intact, the site would not have gone fully dark for days. In a correctly independent N+1 or 2N design, a single fire zone should not be able to remove both the normal and the alternate source; the recovery record suggests here it did, which is the clearest engineering signal in the public record even though the ignition cause is still undetermined. The consequence is that downstream distribution (switchgear, PDUs, rack busways) had no source to distribute, and every tenant without independent onsite generation or a live secondary site went dark despite unburned hardware. Restoration therefore had to rebuild the source layer rather than merely reboot load: temporary power and cooling were activated first (13 May) to keep the shells conditioned, then grid feeds were reintroduced building-by-building (Building 2 in the week of 25 May, Building 1 partial by end June), and finally the intended utility-plus-standby topology was to be reinstated with new transformers and UPS and generators demoted to backup, targeted for 17 July 2026. The multi-week gap between temporary power and full grid reconnection reflects long-lead electrical apparatus (transformers, UPS) and the need to re-establish the standby chain, not a software or data-recovery problem. Two engineering takeaways follow directly: fire compartmentation must guarantee that no single zone contains both the primary and backup power paths, and detection/suppression in power compartments must be sized to prevent a technical-space fire from becoming a total-source-loss event. Definitive design conclusions await NorthC's independent investigation and draft cause report expected end-September 2026, after the 27 July–7 August demolition and expert examination.

sourcing.confidence: medium-high — timeline, impact and restoration milestones are high-confidence and multi-sourced (operator log plus press: fire ~08:45 on 7 May, GRIP 1 20:50, partial release 00:35 on 8 May, temporary power 13 May, Building 2 wk of 25 May, Building 1 partial end June, 17 July full-grid target, 27 July–7 Aug demolition, end-Sept draft report; Keppel DC REIT 'no material FY2026 DPU impact' confirmed by DCD). Lower-confidence items: root cause is officially undetermined pending the end-September 2026 draft report; the affected-customer count and damages figures were never published; the 17 July 2026 full-grid reconnection is announced but not independently confirmed; and the 'both primary and backup power destroyed' characterization is an engineering inference from the total multi-day power loss and rebuild, since published press states only that 'part of the power supply burnt down.'
